summary: Iron screwpile tower on a Gulf shoal off Louisiana, lit in 1860 and discontinued in 1965, after a lightship had marked the spot from 1849.

lens.note: Original second-order Fresnel lens; LighthouseFriends names it a Henry-Lepaute lens. Confederates removed it at the start of the Civil War, about 1861, and the original lens was recovered in 1865 (LighthouseFriends).

structures.note: Skeletal iron tower on eight screwpiles; the archive gives 105 ft to the lantern and LighthouseFriends 125 ft for the tower. A cylindrical keepers' dwelling stood twenty feet above the water.

access.note: The archive lists the station as not open to the public. LighthouseFriends says the Coast Guard owns it and the tower is closed.

visit.note: Abandoned offshore structure; the archive lists it as not open to the public. LighthouseFriends' notes describe an aerial look, on a visit the page does not date, in which only the upper portion of the dwelling was visible. LighthouseFriends says it is best seen by boat or plane.

events.note: Converted revenue cutter McLane, renamed Pleasonton, on station on Ship Shoal as a lightship from 29 Dec 1849 (LighthouseFriends)
Iron screwpile tower assembled in Philadelphia, shipped and erected; the archive gives 1859 as establishment and original lens year
Light first activated at sunset on 29 February 1860 (LighthouseFriends)
About 1861, at the start of the war: Confederates removed the lens and rotating apparatus and took them to Berwick (LighthouseFriends)
Union forces returned the tower to service on 10 November 1864 with a new lens
Lighthouse Board notice in the New Orleans Tribune, May and June 1865, uses Ship Shoal Light as a reference point
Several people paralyzed by lead-based red paint tainting the cistern water; tower stripped and coated with coal tar
Severe cyclone in October; oil thrown out of the reservoirs, lamps out for six hours (LighthouseFriends)
Seabed washed away; tower developed a considerable lean to the northeast (LighthouseFriends)
Attack on Fred Leach by a stranger, James Woods, with a hatchet; keepers shot and the stranger barricaded in the tower (LighthouseFriends; newspapers not named)
Granite blocks from Fort Pickens, Florida, placed around the tower; work completed (Board report for fiscal 1896)
Plans and specifications for metal repairs prepared; bids asked by advertisement (Board report for fiscal 1900)
Metal work for repairs delivered in March 1901; tower scaled and painted (Board report for fiscal 1901)
Keeper John McNamara and assistants William H. Oliver, Frank J. LeBouf and Eugene F. Burke commended by the Secretary of Commerce for work during the September 1915 Gulf hurricane (Bulletin 1915)
First assistant F. Z. Cuvillier and second assistant Thomas Broxson assisted a disabled motor boat drifting out to Atchafalaya Bay, 5 January (year from the 1923 Bulletin volume)
Tidal wave at the station on 13 March; the wave reached a 12-foot mark (Bulletin issue of 1924)

Hurricane of 24-25 August 1926 (Bulletin says "August"; the passage gives 24 and 25 August in the same item); centred west of Timbalier Lighthouse; wharves, boathouses, tie-rods and riprap at Ship Shoal need extensive repairs
Station automated; the tower by then leaned noticeably (LighthouseFriends)

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The archive gives 1859 as the year the station and tower were established and the original lens installed. LighthouseFriends says the light was first activated at sunset on 29 February 1860. The story gives 1860 for the first light and 1859 for establishment.
The archive gives 105 feet from base to lantern centre and 105 feet above mean high water. LighthouseFriends says the sloping tower rose to 125 feet. The story gives both.

The archive lists Charles S. Simmons for 1859-1860 and William Croft for 1860-1861. LighthouseFriends names Croft as head keeper when the light was first lit in February 1860. The archive's dates are years only, so the disagreement is not resolved.

notes_for_editor: Verification pass 2026-10-28: the 1915 Bulletin's lead-in (read in full now) ties the commendations to the September 1915 Gulf hurricanes, and the story says so. The 1926 Bulletin's 'August hurricane' is 24-25 August; the story gives August 1926. Ownership (Coast Guard) and the aerial-look note from LighthouseFriends are now in Today, replacing an earlier 'no source describes a visit' line that was wrong. The 1923 Bulletin's 'Brox~son' is OCR; the name is matched to the archive's William Thomas Broxson by year and station, and the image was not opened. The 1924 and 1926 Bulletin passages were read in OCR; the 1924 item gives 13 March with 'the keepers at Ship Shoal ... heard a roaring noise from southwest', and reads '12-foot mark at station'. Board reports for 1896, 1900 and 1901 were read in the corpus OCR (scan pp. 135, 154, 190). The 1896 entry is a contract 'for transporting granite blocks from Fort Pickens'; the story says so. The 1865 Tribune notice was read on the 8 June 1865 page only; the story does not say May. The notice describes a wreck (a schooner), as an obstacle to navigators. A Tribune Lighthouse notice of 3 November 1864 (uncited, found while checking the 1864 return) reads 'Thursday, the 16th of November' in OCR; the weekday fits 10 November 1864, which matches LighthouseFriends' date, so the OCR '16th' is probably wrong. Not used. The roster matches roster.py output exactly: 265 lines, of which 264 are dated and 'Ira Winn' (Contractor, no years) is not. The story says so. The 1882 attack and the 1868 cyclone, the 1866 paint episode, the 1864 return and the Berwick plans are LighthouseFriends alone (not in the corpus for the Board years 1852-1890); the notes already say so. The 1856 Last Island hurricane is context from LighthouseFriends, not a Ship Shoal event; the story frames it as Last Island. Ownership by the Coast Guard (LighthouseFriends) is the only source for it here; the archive does not give owner.
